newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary secondary bond yields seen rising slightly.
newsitem.headline: Hungary secondary bond yields seen rising slightly.

text.p: Hungary's government securities yields have been hardly affected by Friday's disappointing June inflation figure but bond yields on the secondary market may rise slightly this week, analysts said on Monday.
The 18.7 percent year-on-year consumer price index figure, published by the statistical office surprised the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) which had expected a figure between 17.4 and 17.8 percent.
But analysts said the inflation rise, which broke an 18-month declining trend, had little impact on the government bond market as expectations for an inflation rise in the summer had been widespread.
Food prices which were unusually low one year ago, pushed up June's inflation figure, but a declining trend was likely to return in the next few months, analysts said.
"People rather concentrate on the December inflation figure," said Tamas Puskas of Raiffeisen Securities.
The yields on government bonds, which have maturities of over one year, rose only a few basis points following the release of the CPI figure, analysts said.

"I can imagine a rise of some five to 15 basis points in the next one or two weeks," said Attila Torok of Postabank Securities. "As for the shorter papers (Treasury bills with up to one year maturity)... I would rather expect a stagnation."

He said that following the CPI figure, the NBH was unlikely to continue in the next three or four weeks a trend of cutting its repo rates, or to reduce the 20.01 percent yield on its one year bonds, which are sold continuously.
Analysts said that bond yields on the secondary market were kept high by weak demand for securities with longer maturities.
"Many people explain this by the fact that the (1998) elections are near," Puskas said, adding that investors felt some uncertainty over the longer term outlook for inflation.
Torok said he hoped the June CPI figure would not have a negative impact on talks in the Interest Coordination Council on next year's price and wages.
"(The higher than expected figure) may make employees even more stubborn than now and due to that the government may not be able to agree on a low inflation figure."
The government plans to reduce an about 18 percent average inflation figure forecast for this year to 13.5 percent in 1998.
